name: Stonehenge
description: A prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, built in stages between roughly 3100 and 1600 BC. A UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986) of central importance to British archaeology, it is also a focus of folklore and modern pagan and druidic ceremony.
full_description: Stonehenge is a Neolithic and Bronze Age megalithic monument standing on Salisbury Plain about 2 miles (3 km) west of Amesbury, Wiltshire, England. The visible monument consists of a circular outer ring of vertical sarsen standing stones (each ~ 4 m / 13 ft tall), each pair capped by a horizontal lintel, with an inner horseshoe of sarsen trilithons and arrangements of smaller bluestones. Construction unfolded across at least three major stages between approximately 3100 BC and 1600 BC. The bluestones, weighing up to 4 tonnes each, were transported approximately 240 km from the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales — a logistical feat unmatched among contemporary monuments. The larger sarsens are now traced by 2020 isotopic analysis to West Woods near Marlborough, ~ 25 km north. Stonehenge has attracted major archaeological investigation since William Stukeley's 18th-century surveys; modern interpretations include astronomical alignment (notably the summer-solstice sunrise and winter-solstice sunset axis), funerary use (Mike Parker Pearson's Stonehenge Riverside Project found extensive cremation burials), and use as a healing site (Geoffrey Wainwright and Timothy Darvill, drawing on the Welsh bluestone provenance). It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. In folklore, Stonehenge is connected to Merlin (Geoffrey of Monmouth, c. 1136), the Devil, and the druids; modern druids and pagans use the site for solstice and equinox observances.

aliases.name: Stanenges / Stanhenges
aliases.meaning: Possibly 'hanging stones'; recorded by 11th-12th century writers

origin: A single monument on Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, England.

etymology.origin: Old English; first attested as 'Stanenges' or 'Stanheng' in 11th-12th century sources.
etymology.meaning: Generally interpreted as 'hanging stones' (stan = stone; henge from hengen, 'hanging' or 'gibbet'), a reference to the lintels suspended above the standing stones.
etymology.first_use: 11th–12th century, in Old English and Anglo-Latin sources

timeline.event: First phase: circular bank-and-ditch enclosure with 56 Aubrey Holes; cremation burials begin
Erection of the great sarsen circle and inner trilithons; bluestones brought from the Preseli Hills, Pembrokeshire
Repeated rearrangements of the bluestones; Y- and Z-Holes dug; final phase of significant construction
Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, attributes the monument's construction to Merlin and to stones brought by giants from Africa via Ireland
John Aubrey surveys the monument, identifying the ring of pits later named the Aubrey Holes
William Stukeley publishes Stonehenge: A Temple Restor'd to the British Druids, embedding the durable popular association of the site with druids
Stonehenge becomes one of the first sites protected under the United Kingdom's Ancient Monuments Protection Act
Cecil Chubb donates Stonehenge to the British nation
Stonehenge inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of 'Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites'
Stonehenge Riverside Project (Mike Parker Pearson and colleagues) demonstrates a planned ritual landscape linking Stonehenge and Durrington Walls
timeline.source: Parker Pearson, M. (2012), Stonehenge: Exploring the Greatest Stone Age Mystery

timeline.event: Geochemical fingerprinting (Nash et al., Science Advances) identifies West Woods, near Marlborough, as the source of the great sarsen stones
timeline.source: Nash, D. J. et al. (2020), Sci. Adv. 6: eabc0133

timeline.event: Pearson, Bevins, Pearce et al. publish evidence in Antiquity that some bluestones were originally erected at Waun Mawn in the Preseli Hills before being relocated to Stonehenge
timeline.source: Parker Pearson, M. et al. (2021), Antiquity 95(379)

related.name: Durrington Walls
related.description: Late Neolithic henge enclosure 3 km northeast, interpreted by Parker Pearson as paired with Stonehenge in a ritual landscape

related.name: Newgrange
related.description: Contemporary Irish passage tomb with solstitial alignment

cultural_notes: Long-standing English folk beliefs in supernatural construction by giants or the Devil; modern pagan beliefs in Stonehenge as a sacred ceremonial site.
